meta.description: Buffett wrote it in his 22 January 1969 partnership letter and again in the 2008 and 2013 Berkshire letters - where he credits the line to Ben Graham.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Price is what you pay, value is what you get'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: it is Buffett's own wording, from a 1969 letter to his partners. But Buffett himself says Ben Graham taught it to him. The documented trail.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: b. 1930 · American investor and chairman of Berkshire Hathaway
answer.sourceLine: The sentence is Buffett’s own, in print. It appears — in quotation marks, in parentheses, with no attribution at all — in his 22 January 1969 letter to the limited partners of Buffett Partnership, Ltd., and again in his Berkshire Hathaway Chairman’s Letters for 2008 and 2013, where he hands the credit to his teacher Benjamin Graham.
answer.confidenceText: Verified in Buffett’s own letters — though he credits the line to Ben Graham

source.heading: The documented source

source.excerpt: Market price is irrelevant to us in the valuation of our controlling interests. … (“Price is what you pay, value is what you get”).
trail: 22 January 1969 — earliest use located: Buffett writes to his limited partners that market price is irrelevant to how he values a controlled business, then adds the line in parentheses and quotation marks, with no attribution (collected Buffett Partnership letters, p. 126 ↗).

27 February 2009 — in the 2008 Chairman’s Letter ↗ Buffett finally names a source: “Long ago, Ben Graham taught me that ‘Price is what you pay; value is what you get.’” This is the version the internet copies.
28 February 2014 — the 2013 Chairman’s Letter ↗ calls it “Ben’s adage” and prints the comma form word-for-word, attached to a memory of buying his first copy of Graham’s The Intelligent Investor.

Across Berkshire’s official archive of annual letters, 1977–2024 ↗, the sentence turns up in exactly two of them: 2008 and 2013. Anyone dating its debut to an earlier shareholder letter is citing a letter that does not contain it.
source.excerptNote: In the 1969 letter the sentence sits inside parentheses and quotation marks — the marks of a man quoting someone else — but Buffett names nobody. He would not name Ben Graham in connection with it until the 2008 Chairman’s Letter.
source.rightsHolder: Warren E. Buffett / Berkshire Hathaway Inc.
source.rightsNote: Every documented source for this line is modern and protected: the partnership letter dates from 1969 and the Berkshire Chairman’s Letters from 2009 and 2014, all far later than the 1931 US public-domain cutoff. Berkshire’s own letters index ↗ states that all shareholder letters include copyrighted material reproduced with permission. Short quotation for identification and comment is ordinary practice; wholesale reproduction is not.

author.name: Warren Buffett
author.kicker: The man who wrote it down
author.heading: Who was Warren Buffett?
author.metaLine: b. 30 August 1930 · American investor · Chairman of Berkshire Hathaway
author.bio: Warren Edward Buffett was born in Omaha, Nebraska on 30 August 1930 and enrolled at Columbia Business School after learning that Benjamin Graham taught there, earning his master’s degree in 1951 and then working as a securities analyst at Graham-Newman Corp. from 1954 to 1956. He ran Buffett Partnership, Ltd. through the 1960s — the vehicle whose letters to limited partners contain this line — before winding it down and building Berkshire Hathaway into the conglomerate he still chairs. His annual Chairman’s Letters, published on Berkshire’s own site since 1977, are the single largest source of quotations attributed to him, which is exactly why so many unsourced ones get pinned on him too.

misattribution.heading: The credit Buffett refuses
misattribution.intro: Almost every repetition of this line stops at “Warren Buffett.” Buffett himself doesn’t — and the sourcing that circulates with it is usually a few decades late.

items.why: Twice in print Buffett hands the line to his teacher: “Long ago, Ben Graham taught me…” in the 2008 Chairman’s Letter ↗, and “Ben’s adage” in 2013 ↗. What he describes is a teaching, not a citation, and the sentence is not among the sourced quotations on Wikiquote’s Benjamin Graham page ↗. Crediting Graham repeats Buffett’s claim; it does not verify it.

The 2008 letter is where Wikiquote sources it ↗ and where most citations stop. But Buffett had already used it on 22 January 1969, writing to the limited partners of Buffett Partnership, Ltd. — at a point when the partnership owned 70% of Berkshire Hathaway Inc. (collected partnership letters, p. 126 ↗).

items.who: “Price is what you pay. Value is what you get.”
items.why: The line travels with a full stop, a semicolon or a comma depending on the retelling. Buffett’s 2008 letter ↗ uses a semicolon; his 2013 letter ↗ uses the comma that matches the popular form.

misattribution.truthLine: The wording is Buffett’s, on paper, from 22 January 1969 ↗ — and by his own account the thought is Ben Graham’s.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: In January 1969 Buffett was writing to his limited partners about a nuisance: they kept congratulating or commiserating with him about Berkshire Hathaway’s share price. His answer was blunt. Market price, he told them, was irrelevant to how he valued a business he controlled — he had marked Berkshire at 25 at yearend 1967 when the market said about 20, and at 31 at yearend 1968 when the market said about 37, and he would have done exactly the same at 15 or 50. Then, in parentheses and in quotation marks, came the line: “Price is what you pay, value is what you get.”

Nearly four decades later, writing the 2008 Chairman’s Letter ↗ in the wreckage of the financial crisis, he reached for it again — this time naming a source: “Long ago, Ben Graham taught me that…” He used it once more in 2013 ↗, calling it “Ben’s adage” while recalling that buying his first copy of Graham’s The Intelligent Investor was the best investment he ever made.
detailsBody: Buffett enrolled at Columbia Business School specifically because Benjamin Graham taught there, took his master’s degree in 1951, and worked as a securities analyst at Graham-Newman Corp. from 1954 to 1956 (Wikipedia ↗). That is the window in which “long ago, Ben Graham taught me” would place the lesson — a classroom or an office, not a page.
The distinction matters for anyone citing the line. What is documented is Buffett writing it. What is asserted — by Buffett, credibly, but without a citation — is that Graham said it to him first.
